46.title: A Face Preserved in Gold
46.summary: Explore how a thin sheet of gold became a carefully made funerary portrait—and what its smallest details reveal about burial at ancient Thaj.
46.narration: This small gold face comes from the ancient city of Thaj and dates to the first century AD. Its eyes, brows, nose, and mouth were shaped in a thin sheet of gold. Four holes around its edge suggest that it was attached to a covering over the body. The mask was found among the rich burial objects of a girl about six years old. The museum record presents the care and wealth visible in her burial while leaving us mindful that this object belonged to a real child and family.

story_sections.title: A portrait shaped from a thin sheet
story_sections.body: The maker worked delicate gold into a recognizable human face. Clearly formed eyebrows, eyes, nose, and mouth turn a precious material into an intimate image.

story_sections.title: Made to accompany a child
story_sections.body: The mask was one of many luxury objects found with a girl about six years old at Thaj. The museum panel connects the quantity and richness of these objects with the wealth of her family and their care in following burial customs.

14.title: Symbols Meeting at Tayma
14.summary: Read a sandstone altar as a carved record of ritual imagery and cultural exchange in ancient Tayma.
14.narration: This large sandstone cube dates from the sixth to fourth century BC and comes from Tayma. Its carved ritual scenes include a bull's head with a solar disc between its horns and a full-bodied bull beneath a winged sun disc. Plant designs complete the carved surface. The museum record notes that these symbols recall religious designs from ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, showing how Tayma participated in wider cultural and commercial connections.

story_sections.title: A ritual object made to be read
story_sections.body: The cube's surfaces carry scenes rather than simple decoration. Bulls, solar discs, and plant designs make the stone a layered visual object.

story_sections.title: An oasis connected to wider worlds
story_sections.body: The museum record compares its imagery with ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian religious designs, reflecting Tayma's role in cultural and commercial exchange.

hotspots.title: The carved bull
hotspots.body: A full-bodied bull appears beneath the winged disc. Another face of the cube carries a bull's head with a solar disc between its horns.

hotspots.title: Carved bands and motifs
hotspots.body: Carved details extend across the stone, combining the main ritual figures with additional decorative designs.

18.title: Crafting the Khanjar
18.summary: Explore the handle, sheath, and materials of a nineteenth-century khanjar from the Asir region.
18.narration: This khanjar comes from the Asir region and dates to the thirteenth century AH, or nineteenth century AD. Its silver handle and ornate silver sheath display detailed geometric engraving and fine metalwork. The complete object brings together silver, steel, and leather. The museum record describes khanjars as objects of personal defense and as visible signs of status, honor, and tribal identity.

story_sections.title: Craft carried in public
story_sections.body: The khanjar combines a defensive object with highly visible silver craftsmanship. Its decoration made the sheath and handle as important to its appearance as the blade within.

43.title: A Banquet Survives in Fragments
43.summary: Explore the figures, grapevine, and surviving inscription in a wall painting from Qaryat al-Faw.
43.narration: This fragment of painted plaster comes from Qaryat al-Faw and dates to the first or second century AD. A man with thick curly hair and a thin mustache looks outward from the scene. Above him are two smaller servant figures and grapes growing on a vine. The museum record says the style recalls Graeco-Roman decoration and may represent a banquet. A short inscription on one side reads Zaki.

story_sections.title: A partial scene, still full of clues
story_sections.body: Although much of the wall painting is lost, the surviving face, smaller figures, vine, grapes, and inscription preserve the structure of a larger scene.

story_sections.title: Qaryat al-Faw in a connected visual world
story_sections.body: The museum panel compares the painting's style with Graeco-Roman decoration and cautiously interprets it as a possible banqueting scene.

79.title: Designed to Hang, Made to Fragrance
79.summary: Examine how the linked parts of this 1784 copper mabkhara allowed incense smoke to rise from a suspended vessel.
79.narration: This copper mabkhara was made in 1198 AH, or 1784 AD, and was designed to hang. Its spherical lower bowl held incense, while a matching domed lid helped regulate the release of aromatic smoke. Chains connect the upper and lower parts and allowed the vessel to be suspended. Across the copper surface, geometric and floral engraving turns a functional incense burner into an ornate object.

story_sections.title: A vessel designed around suspension
story_sections.body: The long chains, covered upper section, and lower bowl form one connected object designed to disperse fragrance while hanging.

6.title: From the Sky to the Empty Quarter
6.summary: Follow a 2.75-ton iron-and-nickel meteorite fragment from its estimated impact to its discovery and museum display.
6.narration: This fragment is part of a large meteorite made mainly of iron and nickel. The museum record says the meteorite is believed to have struck Earth about four hundred years ago. This recovered piece weighs approximately 2.75 tons and was discovered in 1932 among the dunes of the Rub' al Khali. It is now displayed in the Man and the Universe Gallery.
